Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], write $A=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j u_jv_j^T$ for its $r$ positive singular values, and set $A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)}\sigma_j u_jv_j^T$. Its image lies in the span of at most $k$ left singular vectors, so its rank is at most $k$. The residual is the sum of the positive singular terms with index greater than $k$; padding the singular-value list by zeros, [F2]–[F3] give $\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2$.

Let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto the row space of $B$, which exists by [F4]. Its rank is at most $k$, every row of $B$ lies in $\operatorname{ran}P$, and hence $B=BP$. Rowwise, $A-B=A(I-P)+(AP-B)$, where the first summand has each row in $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ and the second has each row in $\operatorname{ran}P$. These subspaces are orthogonal, so summing the rowwise Pythagorean identities gives $\|A-B\|_F^2\ge\|A(I-P)\|_F^2=\|A\|_F^2-\|AP\|_F^2$.

Let $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ be the right singular vectors for the positive singular values, and complete them to an orthonormal basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $\mathbb R^n$ using vectors in $\ker A$; set $\sigma_j=0$ for $j>r$. The SVD gives $AP=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j u_j(Pv_j)^T$, so orthonormality of $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ and [F2] give $\|AP\|_F^2=\sum_{j=1}^n\sigma_j^2 b_j$, where $b_j=\|Pv_j\|_2^2\in[0,1]$. If $w_1,\ldots,w_s$ is an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P$, then Parseval in the basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ gives $\sum_jb_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^s\sum_j|\langle v_j,w_\ell\rangle|^2=s=\operatorname{rank}P\le k$. For $k=0$, every $b_j=0$. For $k\ge1$, put $\lambda_j=\sigma_j^2$ and use $\lambda_j\ge\lambda_k$ for $j\le k$ and $\lambda_j\le\lambda_k$ for $j>k$ to obtain $\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j-\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_jb_j=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j(1-b_j)-\sum_{j=k+1}^n\lambda_jb_j\ge\lambda_k\left(k-\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\right)\ge0.$ Thus $\|AP\|_F^2\le\sum_{j\le k}\sigma_j^2$ in either case.
Substitute the bound from step 1.3 into step 1.2 and use $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_j\sigma_j^2$ from [F3]. This gives $\|A-B\|_F^2\ge\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2=\|A-A_k\|_F^2$, proving the claim.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

For finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces $H_1,K_1,H_2,K_2$ and linear maps $A:H_1\to K_1$, $B:H_2\to K_2$,
$$\|A\otimes B\|_1=\|A\|_1\,\|B\|_1.$$
The equality includes zero maps and zero-dimensional factors.

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\{E_a\}_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be any finite POVM. If $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$ and $q_a=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)$, then
$$\frac12\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|p_a-q_a|\le D(\rho,\sigma).$$
The two-effect projective measurement from the Holevo–Helstrom theorem attains equality.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim: By [F5], write each $\rho_j$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues. By [F9] their sum is $\operatorname{tr}\rho_j=1$. The tensor-product basis from [F6] diagonalizes $\bigotimes_j\rho_j$ with eigenvalues all products of those nonnegative eigenvalues. Their sum is $\prod_j\operatorname{tr}\rho_j=1$, so the product is a density operator; the same argument applies to $\bigotimes_j\sigma_j$.

Add and subtract the products with their first $r$ factors changed, for $r=0,\ldots,L$, to obtain $\bigotimes_{j=1}^L\rho_j-\bigotimes_{j=1}^L\sigma_j=\sum_{r=1}^L\left(\bigotimes_{j<r}\rho_j\right)\otimes(\rho_r-\sigma_r)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{j>r}\sigma_j\right).$ This is a finite telescoping identity.

Apply [F7] to the trace-norm triangle inequality for the finite sum in step 1.2. By [F1], [F5], [F8], and [F9], each unchanged state factor has trace norm one; by [F3], the $r$th summand has trace norm exactly $\|\rho_r-\sigma_r\|_1$. Divide by $2$ and use [F2] to obtain the asserted sum.
Apply [F4] to the product output states verified in step 1.1 and the declared finite POVM. The resulting outcome total variation is at most their trace distance, hence at most the sum from step 2.1.

A finite $L$-stage composition contract consists of nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_L$ and, for each $j=1,\ldots,L$, an ideal channel $\Phi_j:\mathcal L(H_{j-1})\to\mathcal L(H_j)$ and an implemented channel $\widetilde\Phi_j$ with the same domain and codomain. Channels are completely positive and trace-preserving on the full operator space, as in [[def-qc-quantum-channel]]. Products act right to left, so $\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1$ applies stage $1$ first, following [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For channels on the same nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert input and output spaces define the **normalized diamond distance**
$$d_\diamond(\Psi,\Phi):=\tfrac12\|\Psi-\Phi\|_\diamond,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_\diamond$ is the unhalved supremum of induced trace norms over all finite reference spaces, as in [[def-qc-diamond-norm]]. For density operators $\rho,\sigma$ define $D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$, as in [[def-qc-trace-distance]]. For probability distributions $p,q$ on a common finite output alphabet define $d_{\rm TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12\sum_a|p(a)-q(a)|$.

The **local channel error** at stage $j$ is $d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_j,\Phi_j)$. The **final channel error** is $d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_L\cdots\widetilde\Phi_1,\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1)$. A **final output-distribution error** is total variation distance between the finite laws obtained by applying a declared final POVM to the two output states. A **failure probability** is the probability of a declared failure event in the finite execution history. These four quantities have different definitions and must be reported separately.

When an input is entangled with a finite reference register, include that reference in the density operator of [[def-qc-density-operator]] and retain it through the channel call; the diamond distance already takes the supremum over such references. Channel, state, and classical output contracts are distinct. Cost coordinates for input description and preprocessing, state preparation, gates, queries including controlled and inverse access, workspace, measurement, postprocessing, and classical output are specified separately by [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]] and [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

$$\|\Psi_1\circ\Psi_0-\Phi_1\circ\Phi_0\|_\diamond\le\|\Psi_0-\Phi_0\|_\diamond+\|\Psi_1-\Phi_1\|_\diamond.$$

map well-defined and unique. It is also a channel, with the displayed factor
order.

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and write $\mathcal L(H)$ and $\mathcal L(K)$ for their vector spaces of complex-linear endomorphisms with pointwise operations ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], [[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]]). Let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each integer $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$ with its standard ordered register basis ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). Write an operator $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ in its unique $r\times r$ block form $X=[X_{ij}]$ with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H)$, and define $\Phi^{(r)}(X)$ to have blocks $[\Phi(X_{ij})]$ on $K\otimes R$. Lemma [[lem-qc-finite-ancilla-amplification-is-block-map]] proves that this block rule defines a linear map on the full operator space for every finite $r$. For $r=1$, the extension is $\Phi$ under the canonical unitary identifications $x\mapsto x\otimes e_0$ and $y\mapsto y\otimes e_0$ proved in that lemma.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

A finite $L$-stage composition contract consists of nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_L$ and, for each $j=1,\ldots,L$, an ideal channel $\Phi_j:\mathcal L(H_{j-1})\to\mathcal L(H_j)$ and an implemented channel $\widetilde\Phi_j$ with the same domain and codomain. Channels are completely positive and trace-preserving on the full operator space, as in [[def-qc-quantum-channel]]. Products act right to left, so $\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1$ applies stage $1$ first, following [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For channels on the same nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert input and output spaces define the **normalized diamond distance**
$$d_\diamond(\Psi,\Phi):=\tfrac12\|\Psi-\Phi\|_\diamond,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_\diamond$ is the unhalved supremum of induced trace norms over all finite reference spaces, as in [[def-qc-diamond-norm]]. For density operators $\rho,\sigma$ define $D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$, as in [[def-qc-trace-distance]]. For probability distributions $p,q$ on a common finite output alphabet define $d_{\rm TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12\sum_a|p(a)-q(a)|$.

The **local channel error** at stage $j$ is $d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_j,\Phi_j)$. The **final channel error** is $d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_L\cdots\widetilde\Phi_1,\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1)$. A **final output-distribution error** is total variation distance between the finite laws obtained by applying a declared final POVM to the two output states. A **failure probability** is the probability of a declared failure event in the finite execution history. These four quantities have different definitions and must be reported separately.

When an input is entangled with a finite reference register, include that reference in the density operator of [[def-qc-density-operator]] and retain it through the channel call; the diamond distance already takes the supremum over such references. Channel, state, and classical output contracts are distinct. Cost coordinates for input description and preprocessing, state preparation, gates, queries including controlled and inverse access, workspace, measurement, postprocessing, and classical output are specified separately by [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]] and [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $H_i,K_i$ and linear maps $\Phi_i:\mathcal L(H_i)\to\mathcal L(K_i)$, $i=1,2$,
$$\|\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2\|_\diamond=\|\Phi_1\|_\diamond\|\Phi_2\|_\diamond.$$
Consequently, if $\Phi_i,\Psi_i:\mathcal L(H_i)\to\mathcal L(K_i)$ are channels, then
$$\|\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2-\Psi_1\otimes\Psi_2\|_\diamond\le\|\Phi_1-\Psi_1\|_\diamond+\|\Phi_2-\Psi_2\|_\diamond.$$

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

If $X$ is a nonnegative real random variable on a finite probability space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$
The weak threshold $X\ge a$ is part of the statement.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

For fixed $j$, partition $F_j$ by the finite successful histories $h$ that reach stage $j$. For each such history, the hypothesis gives $\mathbb P(F_j\mid h)\le\delta_j$; histories of probability zero contribute zero. Summing the conditional probabilities weighted by $\mathbb P(h)$ gives $\mathbb P(F_j)\le\delta_j\mathbb P(\text{stage }j\text{ is reached successfully})\le\delta_j$. By [F2] and step 1.1, $\mathbb P(\bigcup_jF_j)=\sum_j\mathbb P(F_j)\le\sum_j\delta_j$.

Let $T_r$ be the number of trials used by the capped repeat-until-success procedure, with $T_r=r$ if all $r$ trials fail. For $1\le j\le r$, $\{T_r\ge j\}$ is the event that the first $j-1$ trials fail, so $\mathbb P(T_r\ge j)=(1-p)^{j-1}$. For a finite nonnegative integer-valued variable, $\mathbb E[T_r]=\sum_{j=1}^r\mathbb P(T_r\ge j)$ by summing its finite outcome weights; hence for $p>0$ the finite geometric sum is $[1-(1-p)^r]/p$. By step 1.2, $(1-p)^r\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, so this capped expectation tends to $1/p$.

Let $L\ge1$, let $H_0,\ldots,H_L$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, and let $\Phi_j,\widetilde\Phi_j:\mathcal L(H_{j-1})\to\mathcal L(H_j)$ be channels for $j=1,\ldots,L$. Then
$$d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_L\cdots\widetilde\Phi_1,\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1)\le\sum_{j=1}^L d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_j,\Phi_j),$$
where $d_\diamond$ is the normalized distance in [[def-qa-34-end-to-end-error-contract]]. For any finite reference space $R$, input density operator $\rho$ on $H_0\otimes R$, and finite final POVM on $H_L\otimes R$, the total variation distance between the two final outcome laws is at most the same sum. The claim is uniform over the reference dimension; no product-input assumption is made.

Consider a procedure with finitely many stages $j=1,\ldots,L$ and a finite probability space of execution histories. Let $\delta_j\ge0$ for every stage, and let $F_j$ be the event that stage $j$ is the first failing stage. If, after every successful history of positive probability that reaches stage $j$, the conditional probability of failure at stage $j$ is at most $\delta_j$, then
$$\mathbb P(\text{some stage fails})\le\sum_{j=1}^L\delta_j.$$
No independence hypothesis is required. If $r$ fresh trials are mutually independent and each succeeds with probability at least $p\in[0,1]$, their miss probability is at most $(1-p)^r\le e^{-pr}$. For a common success probability $p>0$, the expected number of trials capped at $r$ is $[1-(1-p)^r]/p$, which tends to $1/p$ as $r\to\infty$.

An algorithm result contract declares exactly one output type:

- **Classical string:** a finite bit string in a stated encoding. Its cost includes every output bit written and any required formatting.
- **Classical sample:** an element of a stated finite set, with the output law and the cost of writing the sample encoding.
- **Quantum state:** a density operator, as in [[def-qc-density-operator]], on an explicitly named finite register, produced by a declared state-preparation procedure. This does not mean that its amplitude list or a classical description of the state is output.

The accompanying cost record keeps separate: input encoding length and preprocessing; each data-structure or oracle operation; state preparation and its inverse or controlled forms; ordinary gates, controlled gates, and inverse gates; register width and clean/dirty/other workspace; measurement and classical postprocessing; finite-gate approximation precision; and classical output bits. A coordinate that the model does not use is marked not applicable. No state-preparation oracle, QRAM, controlled access, inverse access, or full classical state description is assigned zero cost without an explicit interface.

For the exact continuous-rotation table model, [[def-qc-state-preparation-cost-model]] and [[alg-qc-state-preparation]] specify the table input and circuit procedure; [[thm-qc-state-preparation-cost]] gives the corresponding $D=2^n$ gate/ancilla upper bound. That bound uses exact continuous rotations and gives no finite-gate or uniform bit-time claim. For a fixed finite gate set, [[alg-qc-solovay-kitaev-unitary-compiler]] and [[thm-qc-solovay-kitaev-error-and-resource-bound]] supply a separate approximation and resource contract. The circuit-family coordinates are those of [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

**Inputs:** an integer $k\ge1$, vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb R^n$ with ℓ2 sample/query access, real coefficients $w_1,\ldots,w_k$, and a positive integer cap $R$. Set $x=\sum_{j=1}^k w_jv_j$ and $S=\sum_{j=1}^k\|w_jv_j\|_2^2$. **Output:** an index $i\in[n]$ or FAIL.

If $S=0$, return FAIL. Otherwise, for each of at most $R$ trials:

1. Using fresh randomness, choose $j$ with probability $\|w_jv_j\|_2^2/S$, then sample $i$ from $D_{v_j}$. A zero-weight term is never chosen, so every requested vector distribution is defined.
2. Query all $v_{h,i}$ and set
$$a_i:=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(\sum_{h=1}^k w_hv_{h,i})^2}{k\sum_{h=1}^k(w_hv_{h,i})^2},&\sum_h(w_hv_{h,i})^2>0,\\0,&\sum_h(w_hv_{h,i})^2=0.\end{cases}$$
By Cauchy--Schwarz, $0\le a_i\le1$, so this is a valid acceptance probability.
3. With a fresh independent acceptance coin, accept index $i$ with probability $a_i$ and return $i$ upon acceptance.

If all $R$ trials reject, return FAIL. When $x=0$ but $S>0$, every defined acceptance probability is zero and the cap still forces a finite FAIL output. No normalized target distribution is assigned when $x=0$. All samples, entry queries, random bits, cap, and output writing are charged. [[thm-qa-34-linear-combination-sampler-correct-and-cost]] proves the target law on the accepted branch and the failure and query bounds under its separate hypotheses on $x$, the cancellation ratio, and $R$.

For a finite complex vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\in\mathbb C^n$, put $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n |v_i|^2)^{1/2}$, where $|\cdot|$ is the complex modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Its squared-entry distribution is $D_v(i)=|v_i|^2/\|v\|_2^2$ on $[n]$ when $\|v\|_2>0$. A vector has **ℓ2 sample/query access** when the interface supplies: (a) an entry query returning $v_i$; (b) its norm $\|v\|_2$; and (c) a sample distributed according to $D_v$. For any finite adaptive sequence of sample calls, conditioned on the preceding history and the current requested sampler, each returned index has the declared law and uses fresh randomness independent of that history; in particular, repeated calls to a fixed sampler are mutually independent in the sense of [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]]. Every draw is charged. The interface states the cost and precision of every query, norm computation, and sample, and any preprocessing or storage cost. If $v=0$, $D_v$ is undefined and the sampler returns the explicit status ZERO; it does not return a fictitious normalized sample.

For a finite real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, put $\|A\|_F=(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$, the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Row and column ℓ2 access supplies entry queries, row and column norms, and samplers for each nonzero row and column according to its squared-entry distribution. These real rows and columns are instances of the vector interface above. It also declares preprocessing, storage, and whether their costs are amortized. The common row sampler $i\sim D_A$ has law $\mathbb P(i)=\|A_{i,*}\|_2^2/\|A\|_F^2$ for $A\ne0$, and the column sampler $j\sim D_{A^T}$ has law $\mathbb P(j)=\|A_{*,j}\|_2^2/\|A\|_F^2$; zero rows and columns have probability zero. An all-zero matrix returns ZERO for a request for a norm-normalized sample. All row-vector, column-vector, matrix-level row, and matrix-level column samplers obey the same conditional fresh-randomness rule; every draw is charged. Access to entries alone does not imply either sampler. The access and output costs are recorded separately under [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]], and the distributions are finite probability laws as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]].

This is an input-data structure assumption. It is not a quantum circuit, state-preparation oracle, QRAM, or an assertion that the preprocessing needed to implement it is sublinear. The Tang matrix algorithms on this page specialize to real matrices; no complex-matrix extension of those algorithms is asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

derivations.claim: Put $S=\sum_j\|w_jv_j\|_2^2>0$. The proposal probability of coordinate $i$ is $P(i)=\sum_j(w_jv_{j,i})^2/S$, because choosing $j$ has weight $\|w_jv_j\|_2^2/S$ and the conditional coordinate law is $v_{j,i}^2/\|v_j\|_2^2$. Its target probability is $Q(i)=x_i^2/\|x\|_2^2$.

When $\sum_j(w_jv_{j,i})^2>0$, [F3] shows the acceptance ratio $Q(i)/(kC P(i))=x_i^2/[k\sum_j(w_jv_{j,i})^2]$ lies in $[0,1]$. If the denominator is zero, then every $w_jv_{j,i}=0$, so $x_i=0$ and the prescribed acceptance is $0$.

Multiplying proposal and acceptance probabilities gives $P(i)a_i=Q(i)/(kC)$. Summing over $i$ shows total acceptance probability is $1/(kC)$, and conditioning on acceptance yields $Q(i)$. Also $kC\ge1$ by [F3] applied to each coordinate and summed.

Independent trials miss with probability $(1-1/(kC))^R$. Since $C\le C_0$, this is at most $e^{-R/(kC_0)}\le\delta$ by [F4] and the cap hypothesis. Each executed trial queries the $k$ entries at its sampled coordinate, makes one mixture draw, and calls one vector sampler. At most $R$ trials therefore use at most $kR$ entry queries and $R$ calls of each other type. Initial norms and mixture setup contribute $B_{\rm setup}$; multiplying the call counts by the declared uniform upper bounds gives $B_{\rm setup}+R(kQ+B_{\rm mix}+B_{\rm samp})$. This count excludes arithmetic, acceptance randomness, and output writing, which retain their separate charges. With per-trial success probability $1/(kC)$, [F5] shows the capped expected trial count tends to $kC$ as $R\to\infty$.

then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, both
$$\|A^TA-S^TS\|_F\le tF^2,\qquad \|SS^T-WW^T\|_F\le tF^2.$$
Deterministically $\|S\|_F=\|W\|_F=F$. The confidence bound has no matrix-dimension factor.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be nonzero, $F=\|A\|_F$, $0<\sigma\le F$, $K=F^2/\sigma^2$, and $0<\eta\le1$. Suppose $S\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}$ and $W\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ satisfy $\|W\|_F=F$ and
$$\|A^TA-S^TS\|_F\le tF^2,\qquad \|SS^T-WW^T\|_F\le tF^2,\qquad 0<tK\le\tfrac12.$$
Let $U$ be the orthonormal left singular vectors of $W$ with singular values strictly greater than $\sigma$, and let $\Sigma$ contain those singular values. Write $k$ for their number, $V=S^TU\Sigma^{-1}$, and $M=VV^T$, using empty matrices when $k=0$. Then $k<K$, the eigenvalues of $V^TV$ lie in $[1-tK,1+tK]$, and some threshold-band target of [[def-qa-34-threshold-band-svd-target]] obeys
$$\|AM-A_{\sigma,\eta}\|_F\le F\left(tK+\sqrt{77tK/\eta}\right).$$

derivations.claim: Set $t=\bar\epsilon/(1000K^2)$. Choose the integer $q=\lceil10^6K^4\bar\epsilon^{-2}(1+\sqrt{2\log(2/\delta)})^2\rceil$. This has the asserted $\Theta$ order, uniformly for $0<\delta<1$, and [F1] gives both Gram errors at most $tF^2$ except on an event of probability at most $\delta$. The algorithm's mixture probability equals $\|S_{*,j}\|^2/F^2$, so a zero-probability column is never drawn and its INVALID branch has probability zero.

Since $K\ge1$, $\eta\le1$ and $\epsilon\le1/4$, $tK\le1/2$. On the event in step 1.1, [F2] applies to the actual strictly retained singular values and to $M=S^TU\Sigma^{-2}U^TS$. It gives rank at most $K$ and a threshold-band target with error at most $F(tK+\sqrt{77tK/\eta})\le F(\epsilon^2/1000+\epsilon\sqrt{77/1000})\le\epsilon F$. Empty retention returns zero and is included in [F2]. No gap between actual singular values is assumed.

The $q$ row samples, $q$ mixture samples and the probabilities of the sampled columns can be obtained using at most $O(q^2)$ input queries: each mixture probability sums $q$ known row probabilities and queried squared entries. Forming $W$ uses $q^2$ entries; its exact-arithmetic SVD and the stored matrices require $O(q^3)$ arithmetic. These costs give the stated counts for the description and make no claim to materialize $A$, $S$ or $D$ in full.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be nonzero, $F=\|A\|_F$, and suppose it has the exact row/column ℓ2 sample/query access of [[def-qa-34-l2-sample-query-access]]. Let $0<\sigma\le F$, $0<\epsilon\le\tfrac14\sqrt{\sigma/F}$, $\epsilon^2\le\eta\le1$, and $0<\delta<1$. Set $K=F^2/\sigma^2$ and $\bar\epsilon=\eta\epsilon^2$. For a sufficiently large universal constant in the sample count
$$q=\Theta\!\left(\frac{K^4}{\bar\epsilon^2}\log\frac2\delta\right),$$
the procedure [[alg-qa-34-modfkv-low-rank-description]] outputs a description of a rank-at-most-$K$ matrix $D=AS^T\widehat U\widehat\Sigma^{-2}\widehat U^TS$ such that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, there is a threshold-band target $A_{\sigma,\eta}$ from [[def-qa-34-threshold-band-svd-target]] satisfying
$$\|D-A_{\sigma,\eta}\|_F\le\epsilon F.$$
The ModFKV description itself queries $O(q^2)$ matrix entries and computes an SVD of a $q\times q$ matrix at $O(q^3)$ arithmetic cost, before any later sampling from $D$'s rows. These operation counts use the stated exact-access arithmetic model and do not include unprovided preprocessing for the input access structure.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be nonzero, $F=\|A\|_F$, $0<\sigma\le F$, $K=F^2/\sigma^2$, and $0<\eta\le1$. Suppose $S\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}$ and $W\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ satisfy $\|W\|_F=F$ and
$$\|A^TA-S^TS\|_F\le tF^2,\qquad \|SS^T-WW^T\|_F\le tF^2,\qquad 0<tK\le\tfrac12.$$
Let $U$ be the orthonormal left singular vectors of $W$ with singular values strictly greater than $\sigma$, and let $\Sigma$ contain those singular values. Write $k$ for their number, $V=S^TU\Sigma^{-1}$, and $M=VV^T$, using empty matrices when $k=0$. Then $k<K$, the eigenvalues of $V^TV$ lie in $[1-tK,1+tK]$, and some threshold-band target of [[def-qa-34-threshold-band-svd-target]] obeys
$$\|AM-A_{\sigma,\eta}\|_F\le F\left(tK+\sqrt{77tK/\eta}\right).$$

Let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ be nonzero with exact norm, ℓ2 sample access, and entry-query access, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ have entry-query access and known norm. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, a positive integer $m\ge16/\epsilon^2$, and a positive integer $r$ with $2^{-r}\le\delta<1$, there is a finite estimator using the lower median of $r$ block means, with $mr$ samples from $x$ and at most $mr$ entry queries to each of $x$ and $y$, such that
$$\mathbb P\left(|\widehat\mu-\langle x,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\right)\le\delta.$$
If $y=0$, return $0$ without sampling. All sample and entry-query costs are charged.

Let $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ be nonzero, and define $D_x(i)=x_i^2/\|x\|_2^2$ and $D_y(i)=y_i^2/\|y\|_2^2$. Then
$$d_{\rm TV}(D_x,D_y)\le\frac{2\|x-y\|_2}{\|x\|_2}.$$
The bound is valid even when its right side exceeds $1$.

Run [[alg-qa-34-rejection-sampler-linear-combination]] with $k\ge1$, $x=\sum_{j=1}^kw_jv_j\ne0$, and positive integer cap $R$. Put $C:=\sum_j\|w_jv_j\|_2^2/\|x\|_2^2$, and suppose a proof-side bound $C_0\ge C$ and $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $R\ge kC_0\ln(1/\delta)$. The routine itself receives $R$ but does not test or require a certificate for $C_0$; these are hypotheses for this theorem's guarantee. A proposal is accepted with probability $1/(kC)$, and conditional on acceptance its index has law $D_x$. The probability of returning FAIL is at most $\delta$. The worst-case entry-query count is at most $kR$, with at most $R$ mixture draws and $R$ vector-sample calls in addition. If an entry query, a mixture draw, and a vector-sample call have uniform cost upper bounds $Q$, $B_{\rm mix}$, and $B_{\rm samp}$ in the declared model, their total access cost is at most $B_{\rm setup}+R(kQ+B_{\rm mix}+B_{\rm samp})$, where $B_{\rm setup}$ charges the initial norm queries and mixture setup. Arithmetic, acceptance randomness, and output writing are charged separately; no unit-cost sampling or bit-time bound is assumed. As $R\to\infty$, the capped expected number of trials tends to $kC$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

derivations.claim: Put $b=\|A_{i,*}\|$. If $b=0$, return FAIL: then $D_{i,*}=0$ and the promised input is absent. Otherwise $b>0$ is available from exact access. Run ModFKV with failure budget $\delta/3$, retaining its rank $k$, sample count, and $V$ of [F1]. If the retained rank is $k=0$, return FAIL because again $D_{i,*}=0$. The sketch event of [F1] has probability at least $1-\delta/3$; all subsequent estimates use fresh randomness conditional on the actual sketch. Write $h=A_{i,*}S^T$ and $z=hU\Sigma^{-1}$, so $D_{i,*}=zV^T$.

At stages $l=0,1,\ldots$, set $\rho_l=2^{-l}$, $\beta_l=\delta\,2^{-(l+1)}/3$, and $\alpha_l=\rho_l/\sqrt K$. Put $m_l=\lceil16/\alpha_l^2\rceil$ and choose the least positive integer $r_l$ with $2^{-r_l}\le\beta_l/q$. For each of the $q$ entries of $h$, use [F2]'s lower-median estimator with $m_l$ samples per block, $r_l$ blocks, tolerance $\alpha_l$, and failure budget $\beta_l/q$; use mutually independent fresh sample batches for these estimates. Each row of $S$ has norm $F/\sqrt q$. Thus on that stage's simultaneous success, $\|\widehat h_l-h\|\le\alpha_l bF$, and the explicit vector $\widehat z_l=\widehat h_lU\Sigma^{-1}$ obeys $\|\widehat z_l-z\|\le\rho_l b=:e_l$. Stop at the first stage with $\|\widehat z_l\|\ge(1+32/\epsilon)e_l$. All quantities in this rule are computable from stored coefficients and exact input row norms; no query of the unknown full output-row norm occurs.

Fix a realized sketch and use [F5] to predefine the disjoint finite sample batches for every potential stage $l$. Let $E_l$ be the cylinder event that at least one of that stage's $q$ inner-product estimates fails its tolerance. Fresh samples, [F2], and [F6] give $\mathbb P(E_l)\le\beta_l$. Since $\sum_{l\ge0}\beta_l=\delta/3$, [F6] gives $\mathbb P(\bigcup_l E_l)\le\delta/3$, and [F7] gives $\mathbb P(E_l\text{ infinitely often})=0$. Thus with probability at least $1-\delta/3$ every stage estimate succeeds, and almost surely all sufficiently late stage estimates succeed. On those late stages $\|\widehat z_l-z\|\le e_l\to0$, so $\widehat z_l\to z$. The nonzero-row promise implies $z\ne0$; hence the stopping threshold $(1+32/\epsilon)e_l$ tends to zero while $\|\widehat z_l\|\to\|z\|>0$, and the procedure terminates almost surely, including for a sketch outside the successful sketch event whenever its realized target row is nonzero. On the event that every stage estimate succeeds, it stops no later than a stage with $e_l\le\epsilon\|z\|/64$, because $\|\widehat z_l\|\ge\|z\|-e_l\ge(1+32/\epsilon)e_l$. Hence the stopped stage satisfies $2^l\le\max\{1,128b/(\epsilon\|z\|)\}$.

On the successful sketch and estimation event, at the stopping stage $\|z\|\ge\|\widehat z\|-e\ge32e/\epsilon$. With $x=\widehat zV^T$ and $y=D_{i,*}=zV^T$, [F1] gives $\|x-y\|/\|y\|\le\sqrt3 e/\|z\|\le\sqrt3\epsilon/32$. In particular $x\ne0$, and [F3] yields $d_{\rm TV}(D_x,D_y)\le\sqrt3\epsilon/16<\epsilon$. This holds for every fixed successful sketch and estimate, so any mixture of their accepted output laws has the same bound when compared with the corresponding mixture of target laws.

Form the coefficient row $w=\widehat z\Sigma^{-1}U^T$, so $x=wS$. Its numerator in the cancellation ratio is $\sum_j\|w_jS_{j,*}\|^2=(F^2/q)\|w\|^2\le(F^2/(q\sigma^2))\|\widehat z\|^2$. On the successful sketch, $\|x\|^2\ge\tfrac12\|\widehat z\|^2$, so the ratio is at most $2K/q$. Take $C_0=2K/q$ as a proof-side bound and integer cap $R=\lceil2K\log(3/\delta)\rceil$, then invoke the finite sampler [F4] with $q$ terms and cap $R$. The bound $C\le C_0$ is established only on the successful sketch event; the procedure does not test or require a certificate for it. On every other history the sampler is still executable: if its component-square sum is zero it returns FAIL immediately, and otherwise its finite proposal/acceptance loop returns an accepted index or FAIL by the cap. Conditional on any fixed good coefficients, [F4] gives miss probability at most $\delta/3$ and accepted law exactly $D_x$.

Sketch failure has probability at most $\delta/3$. Conditional on every fixed sketch, any row-estimation failure has probability at most $\delta/3$ by step 3.1. Conditional on a successful sketch and row estimate with nonzero target row, capped rejection failure has probability at most $\delta/3$ by [F4]. By [F5], the finite conditional rejection laws are attached to their countably many finite stopping histories, so the failure event is measurable in the joint execution model; [F6] bounds the union of the sketch, estimation, and applicable rejection failures by $\delta$. Conditioning on rejection success does not manufacture confidence: for each fixed successful estimate its accepted law is already $D_x$ by [F4]. Step 4.1 supplies the asserted total-variation conclusion on that branch. Outside it the routine may return FAIL or an uncontrolled sample; no assertion treats a failed event as successful.

Stage $l$ uses $O(qK4^l\log(2q/\beta_l))$ queries and arithmetic for inner products, plus $O(qk)$ coefficient arithmetic. Summing geometrically to the stopping stage gives $\widetilde O(qK\epsilon^{-2}b^2/\|z\|^2+qK)$ on simultaneous success. Since $\|D_{i,*}\|\le\sqrt{3/2}\|z\|$, this is $\widetilde O(qK\epsilon^{-2}(1+b^2/\|D_{i,*}\|^2))$. Rejection uses $O(K\log(3/\delta))$ trials with $O(q)$ queries per trial; forming its weights costs $O(qk)$. Even the looser $\widetilde O(Kq^2)$ bound suffices.

Substituting $q=\widetilde O(K^4/(\eta^2\epsilon^4))$, the base query bound $\widetilde O(Kq^2)$ is $\widetilde O(K^9/(\eta^4\epsilon^8))$, and the SVD time $\widetilde O(q^3)$ is $\widetilde O(K^{12}/(\eta^6\epsilon^{12}))$. Since $q\ge\epsilon^{-2}$, the refined estimate cost in step 6.2 is at most these base bounds times $\widetilde O(1+b^2/\|D_{i,*}\|^2)$. On the successful sketch, $D_{i,*}=A_{i,*}VV^T$ and [F1], [F8] give $\|VV^T\|_{\rm op}=\lambda_{\max}(V^TV)\le1+tK\le3/2$. Hence $\|D_{i,*}\|\le(3/2)b$, so this last factor is $\widetilde O(b^2/\|D_{i,*}\|^2)$. Replacing $K$ by $F^2/\sigma^2$ gives the stated powers, with all access preprocessing, precision and writing costs charged separately.

**Inputs:** a finite list of $L$ stage compilers $C_1,\ldots,C_L$, each accepting a rational local precision and, when it uses randomized verification, a rational local failure budget; rational targets $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$; and declared stage input/output interfaces $T_0,\ldots,T_L$, including encodings or register spaces. Stage $j$ must accept $T_{j-1}$ and return $T_j$ at every admissible budget, so adjacent interfaces match. For a channel pipeline these are the matching spaces and channel interfaces of [[def-qa-34-end-to-end-error-contract]]. Each compiler is assumed to terminate with an implemented stage, its output type, and its actual cost record under [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]]. The sequential pipeline is run under the same declared cost-accounting model.

**Output:** a pipeline from $T_0$ to $T_L$, together with the budget lists and cost records below. If $L=0$, a single interface $T_0$ is supplied; return its identity procedure, empty budget lists, no stage records, and an auxiliary record charging any identity-interface and allocator work. If $L\ge1$, set $\varepsilon_j=\varepsilon/L$ and $\delta_j=\delta/L$ for each $j$. For $j=1,\ldots,L$ in order, invoke $C_j(\varepsilon_j,\delta_j)$ once when stage $j$ uses randomized verification, and otherwise invoke $C_j(\varepsilon_j)$ once and mark its failure coordinate not applicable. Retain each returned implementation, output type, and actual stage cost record, then compose the stages chronologically. Record shared input/preprocessing, allocation arithmetic, and any interstage wiring, control, postprocessing, or final-output costs in a separate auxiliary record, counting each operation once. Return the composed implementation, local budget lists, per-stage records, and auxiliary record. The correctness theorem gives an additive resource bound from these records under its explicit accounting assumptions; a requested precision alone does not determine an implementation or its cost.

The correctness claim is separate: [[thm-qa-34-error-budget-allocation-correctness]] proves the global channel and failure bounds and composes the recorded cost coordinates under explicit stage and pipeline accounting assumptions. This algorithm does not create implementations or amplify a compiler's error; each compiler's correctness method and cost remain part of its own guarantee.

Let $L\ge1$, let $H_0,\ldots,H_L$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, and let $\Phi_j,\widetilde\Phi_j:\mathcal L(H_{j-1})\to\mathcal L(H_j)$ be channels for $j=1,\ldots,L$. Then
$$d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_L\cdots\widetilde\Phi_1,\Phi_L\cdots\Phi_1)\le\sum_{j=1}^L d_\diamond(\widetilde\Phi_j,\Phi_j),$$
where $d_\diamond$ is the normalized distance in [[def-qa-34-end-to-end-error-contract]]. For any finite reference space $R$, input density operator $\rho$ on $H_0\otimes R$, and finite final POVM on $H_L\otimes R$, the total variation distance between the two final outcome laws is at most the same sum. The claim is uniform over the reference dimension; no product-input assumption is made.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

An algorithm result contract declares exactly one output type:

- **Classical string:** a finite bit string in a stated encoding. Its cost includes every output bit written and any required formatting.
- **Classical sample:** an element of a stated finite set, with the output law and the cost of writing the sample encoding.

The accompanying cost record keeps separate: input encoding length and preprocessing; each data-structure or oracle operation; state preparation and its inverse or controlled forms; ordinary gates, controlled gates, and inverse gates; register width and clean/dirty/other workspace; measurement and classical postprocessing; finite-gate approximation precision; and classical output bits. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

A **heralded procedure** has an explicit finite outcome set containing success and failure, a success probability $p_s$, and a declared output type. For an input density operator $\rho$ as in [[def-qc-density-operator]], its success branch is the subnormalized state $\mathcal I_s(\rho)$ of the instrument [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]], with $p_s=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_s(\rho))$. If $p_s>0$, its conditional output state is $\rho_s=\mathcal I_s(\rho)/p_s$; if $p_s=0$, no normalized conditional state is assigned and the branch is denoted $\bot$. The outcome law is specified by the instrument and the POVM conventions of [[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]].

The contract states separately (i) the success probability, (ii) the guarantee conditional on success, (iii) any unconditional guarantee including failure, and (iv) the cost of verification and of outputting or recording the success flag. An acceptance probability from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] is not itself a conditional-state guarantee. A claim about a quantum state output uses the type and cost distinctions in [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]].

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and write $\mathcal L(H)$ and $\mathcal L(K)$ for their vector spaces of complex-linear endomorphisms with pointwise operations ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], [[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]]). Let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each integer $r\ge1$, put $R=\mathbb C^r$ with its standard ordered register basis ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). Write an operator $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes R)$ in its unique $r\times r$ block form $X=[X_{ij}]$ with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H)$, and define $\Phi^{(r)}(X)$ to have blocks $[\Phi(X_{ij})]$ on $K\otimes R$. Lemma [[lem-qc-finite-ancilla-amplification-is-block-map]] proves that this block rule defines a linear map on the full operator space for every finite $r$. For $r=1$, the extension is $\Phi$ under the canonical unitary identifications $x\mapsto x\otimes e_0$ and $y\mapsto y\otimes e_0$ proved in that lemma.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). The quantifier includes $r=1$; complete positivity therefore implies positivity. No Kraus, Choi, or Stinespring characterization is part of this definition.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

derivations.claim: For every finite reference space, the extensions of $\mathcal I_s$ and $\mathcal I_f$ are multiplication by the nonnegative scalars $p$ and $1-p$, so they preserve positive operators by [F3]. For every operator $X$, $\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_s(X))+\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_f(X))=p\operatorname{tr}X+(1-p)\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}X$. Thus the maps form an instrument by [F1], and $p_s=\operatorname{tr}(p\rho)=p$ by [F4].

If $p>0$, then $\mathcal I_s(\rho)/p_s=p\rho/p=\rho$. If $p=0$, both numerator and success probability are zero, so [F1] assigns $\bot$ rather than a density operator. The unconditional failure probability is $1-p$, including $1$ at $p=0$; it is reported separately from the conditional-state guarantee, as required by [F2].

For a finite complex vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\in\mathbb C^n$, put $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n |v_i|^2)^{1/2}$, where $|\cdot|$ is the complex modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Its squared-entry distribution is $D_v(i)=|v_i|^2/\|v\|_2^2$ on $[n]$ when $\|v\|_2>0$. A vector has **ℓ2 sample/query access** when the interface supplies: (a) an entry query returning $v_i$; (b) its norm $\|v\|_2$; and (c) a sample distributed according to $D_v$. For any finite adaptive sequence of sample calls, conditioned on the preceding history and the current requested sampler, each returned index has the declared law and uses fresh randomness independent of that history; in particular, repeated calls to a fixed sampler are mutually independent in the sense of [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]]. Every draw is charged. The interface states the cost and precision of every query, norm computation, and sample, and any preprocessing or storage cost. If $v=0$, $D_v$ is undefined and the sampler returns the explicit status ZERO; it does not return a fictitious normalized sample.

For a finite real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, put $\|A\|_F=(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$, the Frobenius norm of [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Row and column ℓ2 access supplies entry queries, row and column norms, and samplers for each nonzero row and column according to its squared-entry distribution. These real rows and columns are instances of the vector interface above. It also declares preprocessing, storage, and whether their costs are amortized. The common row sampler $i\sim D_A$ has law $\mathbb P(i)=\|A_{i,*}\|_2^2/\|A\|_F^2$ for $A\ne0$, and the column sampler $j\sim D_{A^T}$ has law $\mathbb P(j)=\|A_{*,j}\|_2^2/\|A\|_F^2$; zero rows and columns have probability zero. An all-zero matrix returns ZERO for a request for a norm-normalized sample. All row-vector, column-vector, matrix-level row, and matrix-level column samplers obey the same conditional fresh-randomness rule; every draw is charged. Access to entries alone does not imply either sampler. The access and output costs are recorded separately under [[def-qa-34-output-and-cost-types]], and the distributions are finite probability laws as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]].

This is an input-data structure assumption. It is not a quantum circuit, state-preparation oracle, QRAM, or an assertion that the preprocessing needed to implement it is sublinear. The Tang matrix algorithms on this page specialize to real matrices; no complex-matrix extension of those algorithms is asserted.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ have the row/column entry-query and ℓ2-sampling access of [[def-qa-34-l2-sample-query-access]], let $F=\|A\|_F>0$, and fix a row $i$ with $\|D_{i,*}\|_2>0$. Here $D$ is the ModFKV matrix description from [[alg-qa-34-modfkv-low-rank-description]] and its success event is specified by [[thm-qa-34-modfkv-low-rank-approximation]]. Assume
$$0<\sigma\le F,\qquad 0<\epsilon\le\tfrac14\sqrt{\sigma/F},\qquad \epsilon^2\le\eta\le1,\qquad 0<\delta<1.$$
Assume countable choice and dependent choice, and model the finite sketch history together with the countably many potential fresh row-sample calls in the adaptive refinement by the joint product probability law supplied by [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]]. After a finite row-refinement stop, the capped rejection sampler uses its finite conditional law; the joint execution law is the countable mixture over finite stopping histories together with any residual nontermination event, on which no rejection call occurs.
There is a Tang recommendation procedure whose sketch succeeds unconditionally with probability at least $1-\delta/3$. For every fixed successful description having $D_{i,*}\ne0$, its conditional probability of a successful row estimate and an accepted sample is at least $1-2\delta/3$. Thus the unconditional probability of a nonzero realized target row together with failure of these guarantees is at most $\delta$. If the nonzero-row promise holds almost surely, this implies overall success probability at least $1-\delta$. For every fixed successful sketch and successful row estimate, the law of the accepted classical sample is within total variation $\epsilon$ (where $d_{\rm TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12\sum_a|p(a)-q(a)|$ as in [[def-qa-34-end-to-end-error-contract]]) of the normalized squared-entry distribution of $D_{i,*}$. A capped sampling failure returns FAIL; no conditional distribution is assigned to a zero target row. The nonzero-row hypothesis is a promise on the realized description, not an assumed ability to compute its full row norm. The failure bound is unconditional; it is not a claim that conditioning on a nonzero realized row preserves ModFKV's confidence. At constant precision its query and arithmetic-time bounds are respectively
$$\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{F^{18}}{\sigma^{18}\epsilon^8\eta^4}\right),\qquad \widetilde O\!\left(\frac{F^{24}}{\sigma^{24}\epsilon^{12}\eta^6}\right).$$
For the final $\epsilon$ total-variation guarantee, the finite row refinement below adds a query and arithmetic-time factor $\widetilde O(\|A_{i,*}\|_2^2/\|D_{i,*}\|_2^2)$. Fix the algorithm's internal randomness and suppose it makes at most $t<n$ distinct entry queries. Then
$$\mathbb E\|M^TM-N^TN\|_F^2\le\frac{\|M\|_F^4}{\alpha p},$$
and for every $\theta>0$,
$$\mathbb P\bigl(\|M^TM-N^TN\|_F\ge\theta\|M\|_F^2\bigr)\le\frac1{\alpha p\theta^2}.$$
For column sampling, assume the analogous probability lower bound on columns and apply the result to $M^T$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

Differentiating finite sums shows $h''(s)$ is the variance under the weights proportional to $e^{sY}$. Any variable in $[a,b]$ has variance at most $\mathbb E[(Y-(a+b)/2)^2]\le(b-a)^2/4$. Thus $h''(s)\le c^2/4$; since $h(0)=h'(0)=0$, integration gives $\mathbb E e^{sY}\le e^{s^2c^2/8}$ for all real $s$.

Suppose a real function $f$ of independent finite samples changes by at most $c_j$ if sample $j$ is replaced. Reveal samples in order and let $M_j$ be the finite conditional mean of $f$. For each fixed earlier history, the possible values of $M_j$ lie in an interval of length at most $c_j$, since averaging the future preserves the coordinate oscillation bound. Therefore $M_j-M_{j-1}$ is conditionally centered in an interval of that length. Applying step 1.1 conditionally and summing over successive histories gives $\mathbb E e^{s(f-\mathbb Ef)}\le e^{s^2\sum_j c_j^2/8}$. Markov applied to this exponential, followed by $s=4u/\sum_jc_j^2$, gives $\mathbb P(f-\mathbb Ef\ge u)\le e^{-2u^2/\sum_jc_j^2}$ when $u>0$ and the denominator is positive. Let $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ have a singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^T$ as in [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]], let $\sigma>0$, and let $0<\eta\le1$. Write $P_>$ for the orthogonal projection onto the span of right singular vectors whose singular values are at least $\sigma(1+\eta)$, and $E$ for the span of right singular vectors whose singular values lie in $[\sigma(1-\eta),\sigma(1+\eta))$. For any orthogonal projection $P_E$ with range contained in $E$, a **threshold-band target** is
$$A_{\sigma,\eta}:=A(P_>+P_E).$$

The choice inside the threshold band is allowed to vary; all singular directions above the band are retained and all directions below it are discarded. The definition is independent of the choice of orthonormal bases within singular subspaces because it is stated using their subspaces. If a singular value equals the upper endpoint it belongs to $P_>$; equality at the lower endpoint belongs to $E$. A range contained in $\ker A$ contributes zero to $A_{\sigma,\eta}$. derivations.claim: Set $H=A^TA$, $G=S^TS$, $B=SS^T$, $C=WW^T$, and $a=\sigma^2$. Since $\operatorname{tr}C=F^2$ and each retained eigenvalue exceeds $a$, $ka<F^2$, so $k<K$. For $k>0$, $T=U^TBU\ge\Sigma^2-tF^2I\ge(a-tF^2)I>0$. Therefore $P=S^TUT^{-1}U^TS$ is the projection onto the range of $V$. Also $V^TV-I=\Sigma^{-1}U^T(B-C)U\Sigma^{-1}$ has Frobenius norm at most $tK$. By the SVD, the nonzero eigenvalues of $M-P$ are those of $V^TV-I$, giving $\|M-P\|_F\le tK$. For $k=0$, use $P=M=0$ and the same bounds with empty matrices.

We record the spectral comparisons explicitly. For a symmetric $J$ with decreasing eigenvalues, $\lambda_j(J)=\max_{\dim E=j}\min_{x\in E,\|x\|=1}x^TJx$: the span of its first $j$ eigenvectors attains the value, and every $j$-dimensional $E$ intersects the span of the eigenvectors numbered $j$ onward. Thus $|\lambda_j(J)-\lambda_j(J')|\le\|J-J'\|_{\rm op}$. Moreover $\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j(J)=\max_{\operatorname{rank}R=k}\operatorname{tr}(RJ)$ over projections $R$: in an eigenbasis the diagonal entries of $R$ are in $[0,1]$ and sum to $k$, so moving their weight to the first $k$ indices maximizes the sum. By [F2] the top-$k$ sums for $J,J'$ differ by at most $\sqrt{k}\|J-J'\|_F$. Pad matrices by zero blocks when dimensions differ. Applying these comparisons to $H,G$ and $B,C$, and using [F1] between $G,B$, gives $|\lambda_j(H)-\lambda_j(C)|\le2tF^2$ and a top-$k$ sum difference at most $2\sqrt{k}tF^2$.

If $k>0$, $U^TB^2U-T^2=U^TB(I-UU^T)BU$ is positive semidefinite. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(PG)=\operatorname{tr}[(U^TB^2U)T^{-1}]\ge\operatorname{tr}T\ge\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j(C)-\sqrt{k}tF^2$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(PH)\ge\operatorname{tr}(PG)-\sqrt{k}tF^2$. Combining these inequalities with the top-$k$ comparisons in step 1.2 gives $\Delta:=\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j(H)-\operatorname{tr}(PH)\le4\sqrt{k}tF^2$. The variational formula gives $\Delta\ge0$. If $k=0$, $\Delta=0$.

There are at most $K$ crossing indices: if $r>k$, then $r<K$ since each of its first $r$ eigenvalues exceeds $a$ and $\operatorname{tr}H=F^2$; if $k>r$, then $k<K$. Thus the difference between the sums of the largest $k$ values of $\lambda_j(H)-a$ and all positive values of $\lambda_j(H)-a$ is at most $2KtF^2$ . Put $p_j=\langle e_j,Pe_j\rangle$ in an eigenbasis of $H$. Since $\sum_jp_j=k$, the nonnegative threshold deficit is $$\Delta_a=\sum_{\lambda_j>a}(\lambda_j-a)(1-p_j)+\sum_{\lambda_j\le a}(a-\lambda_j)p_j\le\Delta+2KtF^2\le6KtF^2.$$ For $k=0$ the same crossing argument applies, and zero eigenvalues can be padded without changing the sums.

Let $P_1,P_2,P_3$ project onto eigenvalues respectively in $[a(1+\eta)^2,\infty)$, $[a(1-\eta)^2,a(1+\eta)^2)$, and $[0,a(1-\eta)^2)$. Both outside gaps from $a$ are at least $\eta a$, so $L\le E/(\eta a)$ and $E\le6KtF^2\le7KtF^2$. This uses no strict separation of eigenvalues within the band.

On the band space, $R=P_2PP_2$ is a positive contraction. Let $Q$ be its spectral projection onto eigenvalues at least $1/2$. In an eigenbasis of $R$, $\|P_2P-Q\|_F^2=\sum_s\min(s,1-s)\le2\sum_s s(1-s)=2\|P_2P(I-P_2)\|_F^2\le2L$. For the last inequality, the high cross block satisfies $\|P_2PP_1\|_F=\|P_2(I-P)P_1\|_F\le\|(I-P)P_1\|_F$ and the low block satisfies $\|P_2PP_3\|_F\le\|PP_3\|_F$. These squares sum to at most $L$.
